name: California
title: 3 bonds are on the California ballot. Here’s a last-minute voter guide to make sense of them
text:
In summary
Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research.


 Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds.
You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass.
Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 for housing and Proposition 38 for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37, is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly.
Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans.


Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest. The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. 
Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you.
Prop. 1: Affordable housing
If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. 
The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless.The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature.
This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election.
Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans.The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans.Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. 
Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. 
Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1. 
Prop. 37: Help for down payments 
This bond measure is strange, novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns.
Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.”
Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment.
Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. 
Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county.What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments.
How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. 
Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37.
He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. 
Prop. 38: Immunology research
This bond proposal would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. 
The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies.
Previous reporting by CalMatters found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. 
Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies.Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists.

name: VTDigger
title: Separate ballot asks voters to decide $54.9 million career center bond
text:
An architect’s drawing shows the proposed site plan for the new facility on the U-32 campus. Image courtesy of CVCC

A version of this story by Lisa Scagliotti was published in the Waterbury Roundabout on Oct. 17, 2026.
For the second year in a row, voters in 18 Washington County communities are being asked to consider supporting a bond to pay for a new Central Vermont Career Center.
But this year’s $54.9 million proposal is dramatically different — and a fraction of the cost — from the $149 million bond that voters rejected in 2025.
There’s one catch, however: Voters will need to seek out the ballot with the bond question, because it is not being automatically delivered in the mail.
First, the proposal.
Creating a second campus at U-32
The revised plan for expanding the Central Vermont Career Center is substantially different from the initial plan the district put to voters a year ago. In 2025, the district proposed purchasing a 27-acre property in the Graniteville section of Barre Town with a plan to construct a 167,000-square-foot facility that would have replaced the center that’s been operating at Spaulding High School in Barre since 1969.
Cost, location and site issues such as traffic and wetlands all contributed to the resounding rejection at the ballot box in a special vote last November, when 60% of the voters opposed the plan.
Demand from interested students and space constraints at the existing center motivated district leaders to go back to the drawing board. For example, the center had 443 applications for the 2025-26 school year compared with just 134 applicants for the 2020-21 school year. That’s an increase of 230% in five years. School officials say the current center can accommodate approximately 245 students, with more than 100 qualified students waitlisted or turned away each year.
With 39 students attending the career center this year, Harwood Union High School is the third-largest sending school to the center after Spaulding and U-32, according to district data.
After the bond failure last fall, career center school district officials said they were determined to put together another proposal. They carefully reviewed voter feedback across many platforms, examined the demand for their programs, looked at the current facility’s constraints, and considered multiple alternatives before landing on the latest project plans.
CVCC Superintendent and School Director Jody Emerson said district leaders decided to take a different approach to considering the size, structure and cost of the project.
The new plan calls for keeping the Spaulding career center in operation and building a free-standing, two-story, 61,000-square-foot facility at U-32 High School. Together, the two career center locations will be able to enroll approximately 450 students.
The new configuration would not only open up CVCC programs to more students, Emerson said, but it would make greater use of both campuses and shared resources, creating more opportunities for students to pursue academic and career education together.
Emerson said that today’s career and technical education programs have evolved to combine both technical skills and academic focus. Students may be working toward entering the workforce in specific technical careers, but they also may be preparing to pursue higher education in their chosen fields.
“Every program at CVCC has college credits, industry-recognized credentials, or both. Students don’t need to choose between career or college; they need to be provided opportunities to explore both,” Emerson said.
The two-campus approach would give CVCC the ability to expand its offerings while making good use of the facilities and resources in both locations, she said. The additional location would also allow the center to expand its offerings in fields including healthcare, early childhood education, construction, automotive/diesel, hospitality, arts and business.
For example, the site plan for the new center at U-32 designates an “animal area.” Asked about that, Emerson said the spot is a placeholder for space that could be used for a future veterinary technician program. “Animal science is likely to be a new program by the time the building opens,” she said.
The spot chosen for the new career center facility at U-32 is now a playing field. School officials say the site can accommodate creating a replacement field elsewhere on the school’s campus.
On the ballot
For the project to be approved, voters across the 18 municipalities of the career center school district need to vote in favor collectively. After Election Day, ballots are tallied in a single combined count. Specific city and town results are not determined.
The career center district includes all the communities across six central Vermont school districts: Barre, Montpelier Roxbury, Washington Central, Harwood, Twinfield and Cabot.
The CVCC ballot that all voters will use has two questions: one asking voters whether they approve of the $54.9 million bond, and another asking voters to approve a 30-year lease with the Washington Central Unified Union School District, which owns the U-32 property.
In addition, voters in the Washington Central district, which covers East Montpelier, Middlesex, Worcester, Berlin and Calais, will have their own local ballot with a single question pertaining to the career center project. They are being asked to approve their school district entering the 30-year land lease with the career center school district.
Bond vote ballots won’t be mailed automatically
It’s important for voters to know that ballots for the CVCC project are not being automatically mailed to all registered voters across the district with their general election ballots. The decision to hold the bond vote for the November election was made too late for those ballots to have been printed and ready to be mailed with the general election ballots for Washington County voters.
In Vermont, general election ballots have been mailed to all registered voters. Those ballots contain all the elections from Congress and statewide offices such as governor and lieutenant governor, to state House and Senate seats, regional judges and justices of the peace. Voters are encouraged to vote using the ballot they receive by mail and return it by dropping it off at their municipal clerk’s office or at the polls on Election Day.
However, to weigh in on the Central Vermont Career Center bond (and the lease question in Washington Central), voters will need to either vote in person on Election Day, Nov. 3, or seek out the career center ballot ahead of time.
Career center ballots are now available from city and town clerks in the 18 communities. To vote on the bond before Nov. 3, voters may request a ballot by mail from their local clerk. They also can visit their municipal clerk’s office in person to cast their ballot on the bond (and in Washington Central towns, the additional ballot on the lease question).
Voters can direct questions to their local town and city clerks.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ school segregation case back in court as judges weigh potential constitutional violation
text:
Attorneys for civil rights groups appeared in court Thursday to try to revive their lawsuit against New Jersey over racial segregation in public schools. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Several years after civil rights groups sued New Jersey over racial segregation in public schools, attorneys returned to court Thursday to debate whether the state’s own enrollment data is enough to establish a constitutional violation.
During oral arguments before a three-judge appeals court panel in Trenton, attorneys representing the plaintiffs urged the judges to overturn a 2023 ruling that acknowledged persistent racial segregation in New Jersey’s schools, but stopped short of declaring it unconstitutional.
The state countered that enrollment numbers alone cannot establish a constitutional violation, and called for a more detailed look at individual districts.
The hearing was the latest development in a landmark lawsuit that could eventually change how New Jersey students attend public school. The case could have far-reaching implications for Newark and neighboring Essex County municipalities, where predominantly Black and Latino school districts sit near wealthier, majority-white suburban districts. Children who were in kindergarten when the lawsuit began are now in ninth grade.
The lawsuit was filed in May 2018 by the Latino Action Network, NAACP New Jersey State Conference, other civil rights organizations, and families. It argues that the state’s requirement that most children attend schools in the districts where they already live perpetuates racial segregation in violation of New Jersey’s Constitution, the only state constitution that explicitly bans segregation in public schools.
According to state enrollment data cited in the lawsuit, an average of more than 270,000 Black and Latino students, or roughly 46% of those students statewide, attended schools where more than 90% of students were nonwhite each year from 2015-16 through 2019-20.
In addition, Lawrence Lustberg, an attorney for the plaintiffs, pointed to decades of “pervasive” segregation in New Jersey’s public schools during Thursday’s hearing.
In 2023, both sides asked the court to decide whether the state was legally responsible without a trial. Superior Court Judge Robert Lougy denied both requests. After more than a year of unsuccessful mediation, a state appeals court agreed in July 2025 to review the ruling.
On Thursday, the plaintiffs argued that the trial court had improperly required them to demonstrate unconstitutional segregation throughout the state’s entire public school system, even though their lawsuit only focused on 23 “severely segregated” districts.
Those districts enroll roughly 15% of New Jersey’s public school students, Lustberg said. He highlighted Essex County, where predominantly Black and Latino districts such as Newark, East Orange, Irvington, and Orange border wealthier, majority-white communities, as evidence of why the state must address segregation across district lines.
“If Newark decides that they want to send their children to some other districts in order to desegregate their schools, they can’t,” Lustberg told the judges. “They don’t have that power.”
That authority, he argued, rests with the state education commissioner.
Judge Hany Mawla questioned whether the evidence was sufficient to rule in the plaintiffs’ favor without a trial, noting that the 23 districts represented less than 4% of New Jersey’s school districts and that experts had offered differing definitions of segregation.
Deputy Attorney General Francesco Ferrantelli Jr., representing the state, argued that the plaintiffs had failed to account for individual districts’ circumstances, including geography, educational opportunities, and parental preferences.
Pointing to Newark, he questioned whether students might prefer their current schools and what benefits they would gain from attending neighboring suburban districts.
Ferrantelli also disputed the plaintiffs’ claims of state inaction, citing existing school choice programs, charter schools, and state oversight. In addition, he argued that the plaintiffs had failed to prove intentional discrimination.
“They plead this case under the theory that they can prove it just by looking at enrollment data,” Ferrantelli told the judges. “That’s the entire case.”
Following the hearing, Lustberg criticized the state’s argument about a lack of sufficient evidence for unconstitutional segregation.
“Today, for the first time, they crystallize this argument that somehow numbers cannot be enough,” he told Chalkbeat. “But that is not consistent with the law.”
Several civil rights organizations not a party to the lawsuit also presented arguments supporting the plaintiffs.
Micauri Vargas, litigation counsel for the New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, told the court that segregation deprives students of opportunities to learn alongside classmates from different backgrounds, and leaves them to grow up as “strangers to one another.”
After the hearing, Vargas and Lustberg expressed frustration about the prolonged legal battle over the case. Vargas also said existing school choice programs remained too limited to provide meaningful options for many families.
“Every day that goes by where there’s no remedy for this is tragic,” Lustberg said. “Students in Newark are going to have to suffer with how long this is taking.”
Retired New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Gary Stein, who helped launch the lawsuit in 2018, called it one of the most significant civil rights cases in the state’s history, and that its outcome could have implications far beyond New Jersey.
Asking the state “to desegregate its schools is not just to wave a flag,” Stein said in an interview with Chalkbeat on Wednesday. “It’s for the purpose of giving those children a better opportunity to succeed in life.”
The appellate judges did not issue a ruling Thursday. They could uphold the lower court’s decision, reverse it, or return the case for additional proceedings.
A ruling in the plaintiffs’ favor could eventually lead to a separate phase of litigation over what steps New Jersey must take to address unconstitutional segregation.
Either side could also seek review by the state Supreme Court, which declined to take up the case in May 2026 before the appeals court had ruled.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: VTDigger
title: Rural Vermont is done being the state’s expendable class
text:
This commentary is by Megan Durling, a teacher and an organizer for Rural Vermont Rising.
The laws coming out of the Statehouse are not written for rural Vermont. They are written to serve Burlington and Montpelier, ignoring how they will affect Brighton and Manchester. That exclusion is breaking us.
Rural Vermont Rising formed this spring in response not just to Act 181 but to the broad pattern of regulatory exclusion that it laid bare. Like so many of our laws, it was written without rural folks at the table, to benefit developers in larger towns while placing new economic burdens on rural communities. It was the last straw in a load that we’ve been bearing for too long.
The truth is: That pattern of exclusion isn’t limited to land-use regulation. It is pervasive, having shaped policies like education for years. Whether closing off public access to the independent schools we rely on or consolidating our small public schools, the outcome of tripartisan negotiations year after year is the same: reduced educational access for rural working families. Our children are the first on the chopping block. Every time.
It feels as if lawmakers are working to depopulate rural Vermont. We know what happens when rural schools close; many of us have lived through it, and abundant national data shows the inevitable outcome. Closing schools leads to depopulation. 
For this reason, we cannot act as if education policy is a separate issue from sustaining our working lands. Without rural schools, there are no rural families, and without rural families, there is no rural Vermont.

READ MORE

The fundamental problem is the core imbalance of industrial society: the concentration of wealth in cities that depend, for their sustenance, upon lower-paid rural workers harvesting resources from the countryside. This structural injustice produces further imbalance in education. Our cities want to upgrade their schools with their wealth when their rural counterparts cannot afford to do the same. And our state constitution demands equitable education for all children regardless of their circumstances. So, for over a century, Vermont has been trying to equalize education funding to provide more equitable education across the state.
And it’s in the interpretation of that word — “equitable” — that our lawmakers have again cut rural communities out of the equation. Their logic goes something like this: To provide an equitable education for rural areas, we must have modernized schools like those in Burlington. But those cost more. So people will have to be satisfied with fewer of them. In other words, the cities set the standard: If rural communities can’t do education like Burlington, then we can’t do it at all. In mistaking uniformity for equity, our lawmakers deprive rural children of local schools while telling them it is for their own good.
And so, as we who live in the sticks so often see, the high ideals of a boardroom end up producing their opposite aim in application: What begins as a pursuit of equity becomes yet another practice of exclusion. As one local representative put it, shuttering rural schools and busing children for hours each day is not equity; it is exile.
The modernization our lawmakers speak of is nothing more than a marketing term for industrialization, the very process that has severed humans from the land and funneled so many of us into cities. Rural Vermont doesn’t need industrial-scale schools with the latest in flashy tech at the end of a long bus ride. We don’t need modernization; we need humanization, which, properly understood, is grounded in local place. And it doesn’t need to come at an exorbitant cost.
The late Wendell Berry warned that modernized schools don’t encourage children “to return home and be of use to the place and community,” but to leave for a career-driven future that is “theoretical, speculative, and mercenary” necessarily unrelated to their roots at home. Berry added that teaching children to abandon their authentic local culture leaves rural communities and lands “open to exploitation, and ultimately destruction, from the center.”
In short, the industrial habits and priorities of a modernized educational model exacerbate our modern social and ecological crises.
We need a radically different understanding of what educational equity looks like for rural people; our communities have been sacrificed at an urban-mandated altar for too long. The gods of the valleys are not the gods of the hills, and as it turns out, the equity that serves Chittenden County is not the equity that serves the Northeast Kingdom. We do not need schools that look like Burlington’s; we need schools that teach our children the value of remaining connected. We need schools that teach our children the truth in valuing place and people where we live.
We will no longer tolerate the sacrifices demanded of our communities for the appearance of equity or cost savings. We are done being Vermont’s expendable class, and we’re not waiting for one party or another to save us. We are rising to save ourselves, and we welcome all Vermonters who love the land and who love their neighbors who care for it to join us.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma State Department of Education requests $4.4 billion budget
text:
The Oklahoma State Department of Education, pictured in Oklahoma City, has asked for a Fiscal Year 2028 budget of $4.4 billion. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A new literacy law and rising insurance costs drove a request for $123.3 million in additional funding for the Oklahoma State Department of Education.
The agency is asking the Oklahoma Legislature for a total of $4.4 billion in the 2028 fiscal year, a 2.88% increase, but the budget proposal could change.
The Education Department’s current leader, state Superintendent Lindel Fields, did not seek reelection. His elected successor, either Robert Franklin or Jennettie Marshall, will take office in January and could bring different budget priorities.
Fields’ administration presented its budget request to the Oklahoma State Board of Education on Thursday. The request now goes to the state Legislature for consideration during lawmakers’ 2027 session, which begins in February.
Most of the requested budget increase comes from the cost of school employees’ insurance benefits, which is projected to rise by $110 million next year, said Kristin Stephens, deputy superintendent of operations.
Kristin Stephens, deputy superintendent of operations at the Oklahoma State Department of Education, attends a news conference Oct. 2, 2025, at Eisenhower International School in Tulsa. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
As the state implements stricter laws on elementary reading instruction, the Education Department proposed bringing literacy training and services to districts’ local areas by opening regional service centers. Otherwise, educators and school leaders would have to drive to the agency’s headquarters in Oklahoma City, Stephens said.
Placing agency staff around the state would cost $7 million while partnering with local stakeholders, like CareerTech centers, to use existing facilities.
“Districts need for us to be more accessible to them,” she said. “We want to lean in and support as best we can. We also want to be able to deploy literacy training and the best methodologies that we can do. There is something about proximity. Proximity matters.”
The new literacy law also will require second graders to take the third-grade state reading test starting in the 2027-28 school year, giving students an early opportunity to pass it. Administering the extra tests will cost $2 million, according to the budget request.
The Education Department asked for another $3 million for improvements to its Oklahoma City building, particularly to improve the customer entry and experience, Stephens said. 
The agency also requested $1.3 million for its operational budget. Stephens said some of those funds would establish a research department within the agency.
“I think a lot of folks look to (the Education Department) as the expert on all things that are going on across the state,” she said. “What families are doing, where they’re going, all of those types of data points, and I think that’s what the emphasis would be for us — having a research department that would have those data points at the ready and not rely on outside stakeholders.”

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers propose $11M fix to restore school sports and activities funding
text:
Wyoming’s new school funding model added more than $250 million in state education funding, including for widely supported teacher raises, to be spread across Wyoming’s 48 districts over two years.
But school districts also encountered shortfalls and new constraints, particularly related to funding activities like sports and theater. The new model resulted in disparities — giving 26 districts an increase in funding for activities, and leaving 22 others with shortfalls. A statewide association projected funding for student activities would take a $3.9 million hit, and warned of cuts, consolidation or other belt-tightening for activities prized by many students and families. 
On Wednesday, the Wyoming Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration advanced a bill supporters see as a good fix for the activities conundrum. 
The concept is to give each district the base amount it takes to fund an essential activities program at the smallest level, and then adjust based on district size. It would cost almost $11 million in Wyoming’s school foundation program funds for one year.
Laramie Democratic Sen. Chris Rothfuss called it a sensible solution.
Natrona County, Kelly Walsh, Riverton and Rock Springs high school athletes celebrate atop the podium during the 2014 track and field Class 4A West Regional at Natrona County High School in Casper. (Ryan Dorgan/Casper Star-Tribune)
What the committee has learned is “that districts were effectively using teacher salaries to support activities because we were insufficiently funding activities,” he said. “The testimony that we’ve heard, the data that we’ve seen shows, in my opinion, that we were about $10 million short, and this ends up with a system that adds it back about $10 million. So I think this is a good approach to bridge that gap.”
The committee agreed to sponsor the bill by a slim margin, voting 6-5. The vote means it will go into the session with committee backing, which has historically lent gravitas to legislation. 
Golf, cheer, speech and debate
After the school funding bill passed the 2026 Legislature, Gov. Mark Gordon let it go into law without his signature, arguing it would strip local control and could impact noninstructional expenses related to things like activities and nutrition.
It wasn’t long before concerns bubbled up from the activities association and districts. Most districts indicated they could rely on carryover funds to support activities in 2026-2027, according to the association, an approach that is “widely viewed as a temporary, one-year solution rather than a sustainable path forward.”
Recalibration committee members worked over the summer to find an activities-funding fix. Jackson Democratic Rep. Mike Yin was the chief architect of the bill the committee passed Wednesday. He worked with education stakeholders to develop it. What he discovered was that the state has long underfunded activities, he said, which he attempted to rectify.

Rep. Mike Yin, D-Jackson, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“We heard from people saying we didn’t want to cut student activities,” Yin said, “and so what I tried to do as best as I could is just model towards our actual expenses for school districts on activities, so we don’t give them less than what they currently spend on activities.”
Yin and stakeholders referred to their bill as a “cost-based-plus” model that would be scalable from tiny districts to large ones. 
It wouldn’t benefit all districts. The formula would result in estimated funding increases for 34 school districts, estimated decreases for 13 school districts and no
estimated change for one, according to the Legislative Service Office. But, supporters said, it would “right-size” the funding.
The committee considered two other options: doing nothing, which would keep the status quo, or advancing a bill to revert the activities funding to the way it was before the 2026 school funding bill passed.
Even though Yin’s bill represents the most expensive option, Sheridan Republican Rep. Tom Kelly supports it. 
“I am typically very averse when I see the larger price tag,” Kelly said. But in this case, he said, the value of high school activities is large enough to warrant the cost. 
Funding mandates and court decisions
The Legislature is constitutionally required to fund Wyoming’s public schools and is tasked every five years with a “recalibration” process. The undertaking involves assessing the state’s school funding model and making necessary updates. 
The latest recalibration came in the wake of a 2025 court decision that Wyoming was violating the state’s constitution by underfunding its public schools and must remedy that. 
Wyoming appealed that decision. In September, months after the new funding bill passed, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled that the state has failed to adequately fund K-12 teacher salaries and properly account for inflation. But the court struck down other portions of a lower court’s finding that Wyoming has a constitutional obligation to pay for school resource officers, student nutrition and computers.
Lawmakers on the Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration listen to testimony June 17, 2025. (Claudia Chavez/Better Wyoming)
The recalibration committee discussed the ruling’s implications with an attorney in executive session on Wednesday morning. Members then voted against sponsoring a bill to fund technology needs, with critics like Kelly questioning the wisdom of adding screen time for young children. The committee also tabled bills concerning nutrition and school resource officers. 
Committee Co-Chairman Rep Scott Heiner, R-Green River, said lawmakers still want to explore funding school officers and nutrition programs, but not through recalibration.
The latest Supreme Court decision stemmed from a 2022 lawsuit against the state by the Wyoming Education Association, which represents more than 6,000 of the state’s public school employees. On Thursday, WEA President Kim Amen said the committee’s decision to table those bills was disappointing. 
“Ninety-three percent or more of our students go to public schools, and we should be funding them accordingly, not based on ‘well, we don’t have to fund food because the court said we don’t,’” she said.
The committee will meet again in December.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 would bring California’s primary problems to Massachusetts
text:
QUESTION 3 on the November ballot is a matchup between the grass tops and the grassroots. The “yes” committee has raised $7.7 million (with the largest checks coming from private equity), and the “no” committee, with less than $200,000, is backed by a bipartisan coalition of unions, democracy groups, and working people.  
Much of the debate so far has been about the credible concerns of how healthy it is to have a small group of wealthy individuals bankroll a law that would make our elections look like the chaotic California elections. In fairness, many of Question 3’s mega-donors genuinely believe in this democracy reform, while it’s also true that some of them spent a lot of money trying to defeat the Fair Share Amendment, which funds our schools and transportation. 
Big money aside, less has been written about the merits and the track record of the election system the question would usher in, with all candidates competing in a single primary and the top two finishers advancing to the November final election. Here’s what the top-two election system produces in California and Washington.  
In Washington state’s 2016 race for state treasurer, a majority of primary voters in the five-candidate race picked a Democrat. Three Democrats split nearly 52 percent of the vote in the primary. Two Republicans, with 25 percent and 23 percent of the vote, finished first and second and took both spots on the November ballot. A majority of voters picked a Democrat in the primary yet there were no Democrats on the ballot in November.  
It cuts both ways. In 2022, six Republicans and two Democrats ran in California’s 4th State Senate District. The Republican candidates collectively won nearly 60 percent of the primary vote, but split it six ways, with the top Republican winning 17 percent. The two Democrats got 22 percent and 19 percent and took both spots on the final ballot. In that contest, nearly 60 percent of primary voters picked a Republican, but in November, they had to choose between two Democrats. 
This is the “top-two” system proposed by Question 3 in Massachusetts this year, and we should reject it.  
Supporters claim the top-two system boosts representation. The evidence, and conditions in Massachusetts, suggest otherwise. As chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, I take the representation argument seriously. Our communities are finally building a bench. More often now, two or three strong candidates of color run for the same open seat.  
Question 3 supporters should welcome that. Yet, under top-two, it’s a risk. In 2012, California’s 31st Congressional District was about 70 percent people of color and more than 40 percent Latino. The leading Democrat vying for the seat, Pete Aguilar, a Mexican-American politician, finished third in the “top-two” primary and was shut out because he split the vote with three other Democrats, while two Republicans finished first and second. In a district Barack Obama won with 57 percent of the vote, no Democrats were on the November ballot because of the top-two system. 
These are just a few examples where “top-two” delivered the opposite of what Question 3 backers claim. Proponents of the California system will say that lockouts like these, where vote splitting shuts a party out of November, are rare. While it’s true that it usually doesn’t happen, it happens enough that the threat of it happening is exactly how money becomes more influential in these races.  
If a party wants to avoid being locked out of November, significant pressure is placed on new candidates with less money and recognition to back out. We just saw this in California, where the state Democratic Party chair asked Democrats who “do not have a viable path” to drop out of the race for governor in order to reduce the real risk of only two Republicans appearing on the ballot in November.  
“Viable path” is often code for money. Gubernatorial candidate Tony Thurmond said party leaders were “essentially telling every candidate of color in the race for governor to drop out.”  
Pushing candidates out may be smart strategy for keeping at least one Democrat on California’s November ballot, but it shows the perverse incentives this system creates. How perverse? In 2022, the Republican leader of the California Senate spent about $50,000 on a mailer promoting a Democrat. The goal was to steer Democratic voters toward one Democrat and away from the other, dropping her below the leading Republican and opening second place for the GOP. We don’t need these perverse incentives in Massachusetts. Running is already hard enough for first-time and working-class candidates. 
Massachusetts wouldn’t be the first state to say no. Voters in Oregon (2014), Arizona (2012) and, in 2024, South Dakota rejected top-two primaries, mostly by about a two-to-one margin. That same year, similar all-party primary measures failed in Colorado, Idaho, Montana, and Nevada. Colorado’s fight looks a lot like ours: Backers led by a former health care CEO raised $19 million, the opposition, largely groups representing working people, raised less than $400,000 and still won via a grassroots effort.  
The promise of a turnout boost doesn’t hold up either. Two studies of top-two (here and here) found no boost in overall turnout. One found that up to 7 percent more voters skip the race when both finalists are from the same party. 
In Massachusetts, the election calendar makes this proposition particularly bad. Far fewer people vote in September. In 2024, 16.6 percent of registered voters cast a primary ballot. In November, about 68 percent voted. If you’re reading an op-ed about primaries, you’re probably a September voter. Thank you for being engaged! It’s true that a small September electorate already picks each party’s nominee. Question 3 wouldn’t fix that. It would give that small electorate a much bigger job: choosing the only two candidates anyone can vote for in November and leaving independents little chance of even making the ballot. Fewer than one in five voters would set the menu for everyone else. 
Finally, supporters say our current system shuts out unenrolled voters. But in Massachusetts, unenrolled voters can already vote in any party’s primary. Ironically, Question 3 would make it much harder for unenrolled and third-party candidates to make the November ballot. Today they can qualify for the November ballot by gathering signatures. Under Question 3, they’d first have to survive the September primary against major-party candidates. That has rarely happened in California and Washington.   
Democracy reform is personal for me. The first time I walked into the State House, I was a 16-year-old youth organizer advocating for our civics education bill with other Gateway City kids. Eight years later, I ran for state rep. and won a challenging primary and general election after fundraising less than $45,000 (California Assembly races can draw as much as $6 million in spending).  
That first session, we renewed our civics push and, thanks to a broad coalition, passed civics education legislation. Democracy is in a fragile spot right now. For too many people, democracy is not delivering, and we have to do better. Many are understandably ready to keep throwing any rock at the system, but we should be wary of big money trying to capitalize on that populist sentiment. The California system threatens to make things worse by further elevating the power of money in our politics and rewarding cynical electioneering.  
If the six- and seven-figure checks behind this campaign aren’t reason enough for concern, look at what the top-two system has produced in California and Washington: vote-splitting lockouts, perverse incentives to game the primary, and pressure on candidates without big money to drop out.  
The lesson is clear: Vote no on Question 3.  
Andy Vargas is a Democratic state representative from Haverhill. He is chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus and co-chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Business.
